item.title: What’s Queer About The Legend of Zelda?
item.content:encoded:
关键词：塞尔达传说，酷儿理论，异性恋规范，Link，性别角色

总结:
1. 许多电子游戏情节公式化，强化旧式性别和异性恋规范角色，如英雄从反派手中拯救遇险少女。
2. 任天堂历史上主要面向儿童和家庭市场，1990年代男孩被 singled out 为主要人群。
3. Tison Pugh 指出，尽管塞尔达传说系列有异性恋规范情节，但存在颠覆性潜力，尤其关注《塞尔达传说》（1986）、《众神的三角力量》（1991）和《时之笛》（1998）。
4. Link 的永久童年使他处于前性欲世界，因浪漫情节永远无法成功而变得酷儿化；他的身份和成熟度也违背规范预期。
5. 《众神的三角力量》中剑的升级带有阳具快感暗示，Link 的服装风格也可作酷儿解读。
6. 游戏中 Link 与敌人的秘密交换呼应酷儿理论对秘密的关注，Link 的近乎沉默让玩家以独特视角进行颠覆性互动。
7. 最终可以酷儿地玩塞尔达传说，寻找非规范欲望的迹象，增加游戏层次。

Even though the tides are slowly turning, many video games have formulaic plots that reinforce old-school gender and heteronormative roles, often featuring a hero saving a damsel in distress from a menacing villain.

Historically, Nintendo has primarily marketed its games to children, with an emphasis on the family-friendly market. In the 1990s, however, boys were singled out as the main demographic. “Despite overarchingly heteronormative plots of male heroes rescuing imprisoned maidens, subversive potential emerges in numerous Nintendo games,” writes Tison Pugh in Journal of Narrative Theory.

Pugh singles out The Legend of Zelda series, focusing on The Legend of Zelda (1986), The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past (1991), and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998).

“Link’s perpetual childhood maintains him in a presexual world rendered queer by the narrative construction of a romance storyline that can never be successfully navigated.”

That subversive potential isn’t immediately apparent. “The Legend of Zelda franchise stresses Link’s connection to the [Joseph-Campbell-theorized] mythic hero tradition in various moments of his games, with many scenes apparently endorsing a heteronormative storyline,” writes Pugh. “Yet many also exhibit the inevitable queer chinks in this façade of masculine puissance, for along their narrative trajectory, their performance of normative sexuality is undermined by the necessity of forever delaying romance in favor of their very heroism.”

Link’s identity and maturation also defy normative expectations: he ages forward and backward throughout his many adventures. In The Legend of Zelda and The Wind Waker, for instance, he is young and elfin; in Ocarina of Time, he spends the first half of the game as a child and the second as an adult; and in Twilight Princess and Breath of the Wild, he is rendered as a young adult throughout. “Despite these hints of maturation, Link’s perpetual childhood maintains him in a presexual world rendered queer by the narrative construction of a romance storyline that can never be successfully navigated,” says Pugh. Regardless of whether players and fans believe the series features one Link or multiple Links across the convoluted timeline posited in the Hyrule Historia, each of these games ends at a moment of frustrated erotic climax.

More to Explore

Are Video Games Like Novels?

Ashawnta Jackson
March 5, 2022
Video games as interactive storytelling? Maybe not at first glance, but as Eric Hayot explains, the interplay between game and narrative is real.

On a more sexually explicit note, A Link to the Past teasingly hints at the phallic pleasures associated with Link’s weaponry. “When his sword is tempered, the caption congratulates him, ‘Great! Your sword is stronger! You can feel the sheer power flowing through your body!’” observes Pugh. Later, when Link receives another sword upgrade from the Fat Fairy in the Pyramid of Power, the eroticization of the sword as a penis is made explicit: “‘Your sword is stronger! You can feel its power throbbing in your hand!’”

The emphasis on Link’s style and self-presentation is also open to queer readings. More recent entries, such as Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, offer Link an array of outfits ranging from his basic tunic to billowy, androgynous ensembles and animal-inspired attire, while earlier games also linked power-ups to costume changes. “I am at a loss to name another mythic hero—from Moses to King Arthur, Odysseus to Harry Potter—known [in-game] for his modish stylings,” notes Pugh. His observation came a few years before alternate costumes became commonplace across the industry, appearing in games ranging from Mario Kart to indie productions like South of Midnight.

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

 

The Legend of Zelda franchise also hints at secret alliances between Link and several of his enemies in Hyrule. Some shower him with gifts, urging him to keep the exchanges secret. In The Legend of Zelda, piglike Moblins tell him, “It’s a secret to everybody.” In A Link to the Past, a human-animal hybrid thief tells Link, “Take some Rupees, but don’t tell anyone I gave them to you. Keep it between us, OK?” Pugh connects these exchanges to a central concern of queer theory: “Secrets—who holds, fears, or divulges them—have long stood as a hallmark hermeneutic of queer theory, for secrets about sexualities simultaneously subvert and reinforce dominant ideological constructions of purportedly deviant eroticisms.”

Link’s near-total silence—he barely speaks in most games—creates further space for queer readings. “Because Link never speaks, players are solicited to speak for him while playing and engage subversively with the unfolding onscreen drama according to their unique visions of the character,” writes Pugh. Ultimately, he concludes, “essentially, one can play The Legend of Zelda and other video games queerly by looking for signs—any signs—of non-normative desire, which adds another ludic level to the game.”

The post What’s Queer About <em>The Legend of Zelda</em>? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.

item.title: What Came Before the American Suburb?
item.content:encoded:
关键词：Hempstead Village、二战后、郊区化、铁路、历史照片

总结:
1. 美国今日城市景观多由二战后快速开发塑造，郊区、高速公路和购物中心大量涌现。
2. 文章通过纽约Hempstead Village的历史，回顾战前美国小镇生活。
3. Hempstead Village建于17世纪，1643年由两位英国人购地建立社区。
4. 该地长期保持乡村面貌，1898年纽约市吞并皇后区后，附近社区不愿并入，1899年拿骚县成立以保持独立。
5. 铁路连接是Hempstead经济活跃和社区联系的关键，火车站带来人流，促进市中心商业繁荣。
6. 霍夫斯特拉大学收藏的历史照片记录了该村市中心商店、住宅、公共建筑和社区生活。
7. 二战后汽车导向的城市设计加速，1947至1951年首个Levittown在附近建成，罗斯福机场等购物中心吸引走顾客，Hempstead逐渐从乡村根源转变为郊区中心。

Much of the urban landscape across the United States today was shaped by rapid development after World War II. The few decades that followed saw a massive development of suburbs, highways, and later, shopping malls. But what did the American landscape look like before the war? What was small-town life like then? A look at the history of Hempstead Village, New York, provides a glimpse of that period.

Hempstead Village on Long Island was founded in the mid-1600s during the period of colonization. Although the area was initially under Dutch colonial control, two Englishmen, John Carman and John Fordham, purchased land there in 1643 to establish a new community. Carman and Fordham negotiated with local Indigenous tribes living on Long Island to purchase the land, and the following year, families moved there to start their new community.

Cranes Furniture storefront at street intersection, Hempstead, New York
World War I soldier with horse at corner of Franklin Street and Fulton Avenue
Businesses on Main Street in Hempstead, New York
Bohack Building at southwest corner of Fulton Avenue and Washington Streets in Hempstead
Carman R. Lush Pharmacy storefront
Commercial block at street intersection, Hempstead, New York
Commercial Building with Greenwich St. Restaurant, Hempstead
Dry goods and notions store with horse-drawn wagon, Hempstead

In a lecture to the Long Island Historical Society in 1943, Dr. Courtney R. Hall explained how Hempstead got its name. Speaking about the village’s history for its tercentenary celebration, Hall stated that the new community’s name “was derived from the birthplace of John Carman, one of the original patentees, in Hertfordshire—a place called Hemel-Hempstead. Carman’s fellow purchaser, Fordham, was born only eighteen miles from that place.” Like many places in former colonial territories, Hempstead’s name refers back to the homeland of those who colonized and settled in the region.

Train stations helped guarantee foot traffic, enabling downtown shopping districts in smaller towns to thrive.

Despite their long histories, Hempstead Village and its neighbors in Nassau County remained largely rural communities until the twentieth century. When New York City annexed Queens County to form the Borough of Queens on January 1, 1898, the smaller rural communities involved, including Hempstead, were not pleased about becoming part of New York City. Nassau County was established one year later on January 1, 1899, allowing these rural communities to maintain their independence from their metropolitan neighbor. Images from Hofstra University’s Hempstead, New York Photographs collection, shared via JSTOR, document Hempstead during this period and the decades that followed, offering a visual record of the village’s downtown businesses, homes, civic buildings, and community life.

Fire Department Parade on Main Street, Hempstead
First Baptist Church, Hempstead
Group by a pond with boat and barn, Hempstead, New York
Hempstead Library Building Exterior
Long Island Rail Road Depot with Horse-Drawn Carriages, Hempstead
Men standing on shoveled Main Street sidewalk in Hempstead after the blizzard of March 1888
Parade in Downtown Hempstead with Decorated Buildings
Brooks Tire Company and Garage, Hempstead Village

It was Hempstead’s railroad connections that helped keep its economy active and the community connected before automobile travel became widespread. As Arnold Silverman and Linda Schneider explain in their research on Long Island’s suburbanism, “[b]efore the development of paved roads and widespread automobile ownership, railroad communities such as Hempstead (a nascent city despite the legal designation of village) served as the focal point of commercial, political, and cultural life in Nassau’s south shore.” A vast network of transcontinental and regional rail lines across the United States got people where they needed to go, and having a busy train station was a real asset to a place like Hempstead Village. Train stations helped guarantee foot traffic, enabling downtown shopping districts in smaller towns to thrive.

Victorian house with mansard roof in Hempstead
Street view of Island Hotel and adjacent buildings, Hempstead
R.G. Powell Undertaker storefront with proprietor
Storefronts on Main Street, Hempstead Village
Buck Storage Battery and Radio Sales Building, Hempstead
Chas. Dreihof Sammis Hotel and Surrounding Businesses, Hempstead Village
Facade of Thomas J. Wylie Old Homestead Hotel with S. Liebmann's Sons Rheingold Teutonic Signage
Hempstead Inquirer Building on Main Street

While automobile-centric urban design took off quickly after World War II, it built on a trend that had begun prior to the war. In their report on twentieth-century urbanism in the United States, Thomas J. Nechyba and Randall P. Walsh point out that “[b]y 1910 the number of registered automobiles in the U.S. had passed the 500,000 mark, and in 1920 car registration reached eight million.”

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

This came quickly to Long Island in the post-World War II period. The first Levittown, an iconic planned suburban community that was copied around the country, was built from 1947 to 1951, less than 10 miles from Hempstead Village. The development of shopping malls like Roosevelt Field drew shoppers away from historic commercial centers like Hempstead. Like much of the country, Hempstead Village continued to transform from a community with rural roots into a suburban center.

The post What Came Before the American Suburb? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.

item.title: How the Elite Learned to Seem Less Elite
item.content:encoded:
精英文化, 大众文化, 休闲活动, 道德合法性, 英国Who's Who

总结:
1. 社会精英不仅物质上控制他人，还定义何为“好”。
2. 研究基于英国《Who's Who》百年数据，分析精英休闲活动的代际变化。
3. 19世纪后期精英很少提及休闲，多为贵族乡村活动。
4. 20世纪初精英转向城市，受知识分子影响，1920-1940年代形成“高雅文化”兴趣，休闲自我展示比例大增。
5. 战后高雅兴趣仍存，但精英开始纳入大众文化元素，展示识别“品质”的能力。
6. 近几代精英更多提及与亲友相处，以淡化势利形象，1990年代起尤甚。
7. 这与英国前1%收入急升同步，精英经济上远离其他群体，道德合法性焦虑加剧。

The richest, most powerful people in a society don’t just materially control the lives of others. They also help determine what kinds of tastes are “good.” Looking at more than a century’s worth of data from the British Who’s Who guide, sociologists Sam Friedman and Aaron Reeves found distinct periods when this meant very different things.

Who’s Who, which has been published annually since 1897, includes 0.05 percent of the UK population. Half are chosen simply for holding a prominent position, such as Member of Parliament, CEO of a large company, or fellow of the British Academy. The other half are picked by a board of advisors, reflecting their reputation among those “in the know.”

In the postwar era, highbrow interests remained popular, but entrants increasingly also listed elements of mass culture.

Friedman and Reeves looked at the guide’s open-response section for “recreations.” Because people’s long-term tastes typically stabilize in early adulthood, they organized their analysis around generational cohorts, based on the decade each entrant turned 20.

Among the British elites who came of age in the second half of the nineteenth century, less than half listed any recreations at all, perhaps showing that leisure activities weren’t a terribly important part of self-presentation for this group. Most activities that were listed in this era, including hunting, fishing, golf, horse riding, and sailing, reflected an idealized version of rural life, carried out mostly by aristocrats at large country estates.

In the early twentieth century, Who’s Who entrants increasingly came from the urban industrial capitalist class. And as the center of elite life moved to London, even members of the gentry shifted how they enjoyed themselves. A particular influence in this era was the Bloomsbury Group, intellectuals and artists who based their self-conscious elitism on philosophical and aesthetic sophistication.

More to Explore

Legionnaires’ Disease, an Illness of Affluence

Katrina Gulliver
November 19, 2024
Legionnaires’ is the first communicable disease of modern wealth, thriving in the interstitial spaces of our built environment.

Between the 1920s and 1940s, the Who’s Who elites developed the set of interests that would define “high culture,” such as music, reading, and “the arts.” Leisure activities also became a much bigger part of elites’ public self-presentation in this period—the percentage of entrants reporting on their recreations grew from about 40 percent of those who turned 20 in 1900 to 80 percent in 1950.

In the postwar era, highbrow interests remained popular, but entrants increasingly also listed elements of mass culture. Friedman and Reeves suggest that elites were engaging with pop culture in a way that showcased a deep familiarity and ability to recognize “quality.”

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

An even bigger shift in recent generations has been a rise in mentions of activities like spending time with friends and family. Often, entrants include these alongside aristocratic and highbrow interests in a way that could reduce the appearance of snobbishness.

For elites of all generations, this became increasingly common starting in the 1990s. Friedman and Reeves suggest that it’s no coincidence that this was also a moment when the incomes of Britain’s top 1 percent began rising sharply in comparison with the rest of the country.

“As elites have pulled away economically from other social groups, there is evidence that they have become increasingly insecure about their moral legitimacy,” they write.

item.title: The Nazi Car That Conquered the World
item.content:encoded:
关键词：纳粹 Volkswagen KdF-Wagen Beetle 战后德国 经济奇迹

总结:
1. 纳粹德国通过“力量来自欢乐”组织推出KdF-Wagen，即大众甲壳虫前身，1938年以“人民汽车”名义宣传，但犹太人被禁止购买。
2. 希特勒本人获得极少数量产车之一，普通民众付款购买邮票却从未收到车，工厂1939至1945年转产军备，战后30年才清偿12万份索赔。
3. 战后英国工程师重启沃尔夫斯堡工厂，1948年Type 1首次真正大规模量产，成为西德“经济奇迹”的象征。
4. 其纳粹起源成为“公开的秘密”，1991年大众承认纳粹时期使用强迫劳动并设立赔偿基金。
5. 甲壳虫全球热销，成为战后去法西斯化德国的世界性标志，但成功叙事掩盖了其不光彩的起源。

How did the Nazi Volkswagen become the world-renowned symbol of postwar, post-fascist Germany?

“Millions of postwar Germans imaged driving away from their past,” writes historian Natalie Scholz, but they were doing so in the “debris of the Nazi Empire.”

The Nazi state leisure organization Kraft durch Freude (Strength through Joy) introduced the KdF-Wagen, as the first incarnation of the VW Beetle was called, with great fanfare in 1938. In a country with little car ownership, the KdF-Wagen was promoted as an affordable vehicle for the Volk (people). It was presented as the automotive flagship of a “racially defined Volksgemeinschaft” (people’s community); Jewish Germans were not allowed to purchase one.

Hitler, the car’s biggest booster, unsurprisingly got one of the very few produced. For everyone else, the promised car never materialized.

KdF-Wagens were supposed to be produced in a new, purpose-built factory town given the utilitarian name Stadt des KdF-Wagens. The enormous facility, later known as Wolfsburg, was planned to produce 1.5 million cars annually. The basic price in 1938 was 990 Reichsmarks (RM). An installment plan meant people could invest 5 RM at a time, receiving special stamps to show their payments. The idea was to fill four 250 RM stamp books and then turn them in for a vehicle.

But here’s the thing about investing in totalitarianism: it’s a sucker’s game. Hitler, the car’s biggest booster, unsurprisingly got one of the very few produced. For everyone else, the promised car never materialized. From 1939 until 1945, the Wolfsburg factory was given over to military vehicles and munitions, even as the regime continued to promote the unavailable civilian car. It would take thirty years for Volkswagen to finally settle the last of the 120,000 claims from those who had purchased the stamps.

After the war, a British engineer led the effort to bring the Wolfsburg plant back online. When production increased for the VW Type 1 in 1948, writes Scholz, “it was the first time that the car as it was originally conceived became a mass-produced reality, populating German streets.”

More to Explore

Papering Over History

Robert M. Ehrenreich and Alexandra M. Lord
September 24, 2025
Efka—the German rolling paper company—was a Nazi regime favorite. After World War II, it was refashioned as a darling of the pot-infused counterculture.

Since it looked like a ladybug, the Type 1 was called the Käfer, which is German for beetle. In English, it was affectionately known as the Bug or Beetle. Names in other markets included Vocho, Coccinelle, Fusca, and Maggiolino. “Beetle” became the official name in 1968. Over 21.5 million were made, a world record for number of units and years of production. While Wolfsburg stopped production in 1974, the Type 1 continued to be produced in Mexico until 2003. (The “New Beetle” was launched in 1998.)

“What has made [the car] well-known and popular, what has made it the top-selling and much sought-after German car is not its history of origins, but the harmony of its technical and economical features,” went a 1952 VW print advertisement quoted by Scholz, who italicized the elephant in the room.

The iconic Beetle became the embodiment of West Germany’s postwar Wirtschaftswunder. This “economic miracle” was a rise from the literal ashes of defeat to a secure place in “the West’s” consumer democracy. But such transformations are only “miracles,” Scholz argues, when their genesis is invisible.

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

That genesis would officially be acknowledged in 1991 when Volkswagen accepted corporate responsibility for crimes against humanity during the Nazi period and set up a compensation fund for survivors of the enslaved labor used in Wolfsburg. (Last year, a Brazilian court found Volkswagen liable for exploiting forced labor in that country during the military dictatorship there.)

The Beetle’s origins were always what Scholz calls a “public secret.” That public secret was also alluded to in an “Auschwitz joke” Scholz heard in 1980s West Germany, when she was around ten years old. She writes that “How many Jews fit in a Volkswagen?” is older than that, with variations going back to the 1950s. The answer is unspeakable, a grotesque mixture, Scholz writes, of “anti-Semetic aggression and feelings of superiority as well as a German consciousness of the Holocaust—possibly accompanied by feelings of shame.”

item.title: The Chinese-Only Schools of the Jim Crow South
item.content:encoded:
关键词：Gong Lum v. Rice、密西西比三角洲华人、种族隔离、 Baptist mission schools、教育隔离

总结:
1. 1924年Gong Lum v. Rice案中，初级法院最初裁定华人儿童可与白人同校，但很快被推翻，最高法院依据州宪法维持“白人”与“有色人种”分开办学。
2. 19世纪70年代华人作为农业工人来到密西西比三角洲，形成以家庭为中心的乡村聚居区，处于白人与黑人之间的模糊种族地位。
3. 华人领袖在法律上主张自己不应被归为“有色人种”，并努力与白人友好相处，采用“白人”行为模式，以区别于非洲裔美国人。
4. 当Rosedale白人反对华人学生进入白人学校并引发诉讼后，华人转而依靠浸信会 mission schools，在20世纪30年代建立多所教会学校，主要教授英语并展示自身文化以争取白人接纳。
5. 这些 mission schools 帮助华人获得社会接纳，但代价是与非洲裔及混血儿童保持距离，部分混血儿被排除在外，只能就读黑人公立或天主教学校。
6. 后来一些华人家长将年长子女送往加州、得州等地公立学校，直到20世纪40年代中期三角洲白人学校开始种族融合；这段历史对理解美国教育隔离与种族不平等至关重要。

The initial court ruling seemed like a victory for Chinese Americans in the Mississippi Delta: Chinese children could attend school with their white peers, said the judge. But the Mississippi Circuit Court’s decision in the 1924 case was soon overturned.

The first judge had accepted that Chinese students should not have to share facilities with African Americans, whom he called “wholly different from them in racial characteristics.”

Yet the Supreme Court ultimately pointed to the state Constitution’s stipulation that “separate schools shall be maintained for children of the white and colored races.” And “[y]ellow, after all, was a color,” as educational researcher Sieglinde Lim de Sánchez remarks.

Decades before Mendez v. Westminster and the landmark Brown v. Board of Education, the case of Gong Lum, et al. v. Rice shows the ideological contradictions of school segregation.

When petitioner Gong Lum fought for his daughter to be admitted to a white school, his legal argument was that the Chinese should not be counted as “colored.”

Chinese immigrants came to the Delta as agricultural workers in the 1870s—soon forming family-centered rural enclaves that contrasted with the bachelor society of urban Chinatowns.

While they lived in predominantly African American areas, Mississippi Chinese “resisted legal and customary efforts to conflate their status with that of blacks” under Jim Crow laws—a sign of the unclear racial status of Southerners who were neither white nor African American.

Community leaders “consulted with sympathetic whites who urged them to adopt ‘white’ behavior patterns in their dealings with African Americans,” explains Lim de Sánchez.

When petitioner Gong Lum fought for his daughter to be admitted to a white school, his legal argument was that the Chinese should not be counted as “colored.”

“If a Chinese family lived in one of the smaller Delta town[s], and was good friends with the Bok Guey [whites], they’d let you go to their school,” longtime Delta resident Jack Chow recalled in an interview with Lim de Sánchez.

As Chinese parents began boarding their children with Rosedale families or moving into the district, the white townspeople of Rosedale pushed back—resulting in the court case that legally barred Chinese American students from accessing white-only schools.

Sending their children to segregated African American schools was out of the question for Chinese community leaders, who considered the matter “an issue of crucial importance.”

Instead, the Mississippi Chinese found a way to have schools of their own. Baptist congregations, eager to proselytize to the Chinese community, were already offering nighttime classes to teach adults English and encourage “Americanized” domestic habits.

“The Chinese gradually realized the missions could be crucial institutional vehicles in facilitating their drive toward full participation in white society, for they provided a forum to demonstrate to whites that they were not heathen,” Lim de Sánchez notes.

With Chinese parents’ backing, local Baptist churches opened various educational missions in the 1930s, including a single-story “shotgun shack” backed by the First Baptist Church of Greenville and a school under Rosedale Consolidated School’s Chinese Department.

More to Explore

Brown v. Board of Education: Annotated

Liz Tracey
May 17, 2023
The 1954 Supreme Court decision, based on the Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution, declared that “separate but equal” has no place in education.

One notable institution was the Cleveland Chinese Mission School, which opened in 1937 with donations from Chinese communities as far away as New York and San Francisco and even attracted out-of-state Chinese students from places like Tennessee and Arkansas.

Though Chinese community leaders supported after-school programs to impart Chinese culture, the schools were established mainly to teach English. They did not necessarily offer high-quality instruction—the Cleveland school was not even accredited by the state.

Still, mission schools allowed Mississippi Chinese to gain social acceptance in the racially segregated South, as they could “demonstrat[e] to whites that they possessed a cultural heritage and ‘innate’ capabilities that differed from African Americans.”

This came at the expense of Chinese Americans’ relationships with their African American neighbors, as they feared “any association might reverse the acceptance they had spent years trying to achieve within the larger Delta white society,” Lim de Sánchez says.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Interracial families were ostracized, and mixed-race children were excluded from the Baptist mission schools. Instead, they attended the local African American public or Catholic schools.

Eventually, Chinese parents in the Delta realized the limitations of a separate school system, and some opted to send their older children to public schools in other states—such as California and Texas—until white Delta schools began racial integration in the mid-1940s.

But recovering the pre–World War II history of these mission schools in the South is critical to “the formation and understanding of issues of educational segregation as well as racial inequality in the United States as a whole,” Lim de Sánchez concludes.

Despite the discrimination they faced, Mississippi Chinese “successfully established alternative schools that paralleled the exclusionary white educational institutions.”

item.title: Why Is Raja Ravi Varma’s Art So Valuable Today?
item.content:encoded:
关键词：Raja Ravi Varma，印度艺术市场，拍卖纪录，印度教神像海报，Hindutva政治

总结:
1. 2026年4月，Raja Ravi Varma的《Yashoda and Krishna》以16.7亿卢比（1790万美元）成交，创印度艺术品拍卖最高纪录，远超MF Husain此前1380万美元的纪录。
2. Ravi Varma（1848年生）出身Travancore王室，是首位以西方油画风格描绘印度题材的印度艺术家，也是现代印度绘画先驱。
3. 他通过自己的印刷厂大量生产石版画，定义了印度教宗教图像，被Jacobsen称为“神像海报产业”的奠基人。
4. Pinney指出其女性形象帮助塑造了印度民族认同，但也与印度教民族主义（Hindutva）的传播密切相关。
5. 此次高价成交或反映近年来印度Hindutva政治影响力上升，历史艺术的流行亦随之复兴。

In April, a new record was set for the Indian art market when a painting by renowned Indian artist Raja Ravi Varma, created in the late nineteenth century, became the most expensive Indian artwork ever sold at auction. Yashoda and Krishna sold for 1.67 billion rupees ($17.9 million), far surpassing the previous record, held by modernist painter MF Husain’s Untitled (Gram Yatra), which sold for $13.8 million in 2025.

It’s noteworthy that an artwork painted in a predominantly Western-influenced style and depicting an overtly religious subject could command such a high price in a market where works by modernist artists have reigned for decades.

Professor Knut A. Jacobsen argues that Ravi Varma was the undisputed founder of a genre he terms the “God poster industry.”

Ravi Varma, born in 1848, belonged to the royal family of Travancore, a kingdom in what is now the southern Indian state of Kerala. He challenged caste and class hierarchies by choosing to be a painter and became the first Indian artist to paint Indian subjects in a Western style. He is widely regarded as a pioneer of modern Indian painting and one of the most influential artists from the subcontinent. Varma’s popularity grew at the height of the British Empire in India, as Western-style oil painting, with its emphasis on depth and chiaroscuro, gained prominence in the country. He began by painting grand portraits of royal and noble figures from across India and later turned to scenes from Hindu mythology in his work, becoming the first Indian artist to gain a nationwide audience.

In “Indian Painting from 1825 to 1900,” published in the 2011 volume Masters of Indian Painting II: 1650-1900, independent researcher Tryna Lyons describes Varma as “the first of India’s ‘gentleman artists’” because, “at the time that he made the daring decision to learn the craft of painting, artists enjoyed roughly the same social status as tailors and cabinet makers.”

By adopting the expensive medium of oil paint, Ravi Varma popularized the foreign art of representation, which, according to Lyons, was “primarily concerned with duplicating the observed world.” Yet it was his “theatrical interpretations of Sanskrit epic and drama” that glorified scenes from Hindu mythology and made him a household name.

His paintings and oleographs, produced by his own printing press, came to define Hindu religious iconography in India. Professor Knut A. Jacobsen, in his 2004 article, “The Child Manifestation of Śiva in Contemporary Hindu Popular Prints,” published in Numen, argues that Ravi Varma was the undisputed founder of a genre he terms the “God poster industry.” This genre took on a vibrant life of its own and remains popular today.

Jacobsen writes: “During the last one hundred years colourful prints of the Hindu gods, usually called God posters, have become one of the most visible aspects of popular religious culture in South Asia. There is hardly a Hindu home, shop or workshop without one print or more on the wall or on the puja table.”  He connects this popularity to sacred narratives, noting that “some of the posters do indeed illustrate sacred narratives found in the Saiva Puranas. The artists re-actualise themes from the Puranas.”

Despite his focus on Hindu religious iconography, Lyons argues that Ravi Varma also embraced the ideal of “harmony in diversity,” which came to define modern India. She cites his participation in the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where he displayed ten works featuring female subjects from across India in regional dress.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Anthropologist and art historian Christopher Pinney, however, offers a different interpretation in his 1997 article, “The Nation (Un)Pictured? Chromolithography and ‘Popular’ Politics in India, 1878–1995,” published in Critical Inquiry. He identifies the Ravi Varma Press as a main propagator of Hindu religious ideals and political ideas. He writes:

The ubiquity of Hindu propaganda is a necessary mark of the popularity of religious nationalism, and the proliferation and invasiveness of the imagery contriv[es] a sense of the irresistible tide of Hindutva … Both the Chitrashala Press and the Ravi Varma Press (which started in 1894) found themselves at the nexus of a political ferment in western and northern India. A diverse set of individuals and groups were involved in strategies which mobilised both two- and three-dimensional imagery in their attempts to control public spaces. In agitations such as that over Cow Protection and Tilak’s co-optation of the Ganpati festival, there was a less visible, but no less potent, colonisation of private domestic spaces by the products of early presses which ran parallel to the much better known struggles over public spaces and signs.

The “new media,” which included oleographs, captured the popular imagination in the early 1890s. British officials at the time saw this development as the emergence of “print nationalism.” Pinney argues that the female figures in Ravi Varma’s work helped drive its proliferation. He cites the painting Tarini, “in which it has been suggested an enveloping sari assumes the form of India (though curiously an India without Bengal). More than any other individual, Ravi Varma crystallized a putative Indian national identity in various feminine figures.”

Raja Ravi Varma’s iconic status in the Indian art pantheon is undeniable. However, the record-breaking sale raises a question: Why now? The high-value sale of his painting in 2026 may reflect the changing political landscape in India, where Hindutva politics has gained influence in recent years. After all, history repeats itself, and the popularity of historical art can, too.

The post Why Is Raja Ravi Varma’s Art So Valuable Today? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.

item.title: A Brief History of Women’s Underwear
item.content:encoded:
关键词：怀俄明大学、内衣档案、女性内衣、时尚史、社会变迁

总结:
1. 怀俄明大学收藏了大量女性内衣，从内战时期到60年代，每件都有故事。
2. 这些藏品是该校历史服装收藏的一部分，展现了科学创新和社会进步。
3. 文章按时间线展示袜子、内衣等演变，如维多利亚时代、一战、20年代、40年代尼龙发明等。
4. 内衣变化反映女性生活：从隐藏到显露，从束缚到自由，如灯笼裤、连体衣、短裙搭配。
5. 二战后迪奥“新Look”带回曲线美，需要紧身胸衣和衬裙。
6. 通过虚拟浏览可拼出完整女性 outfit，讲述真实故事。

The University of Wyoming is home to an archive of undergarments. And its collection of unmentionables—from the simple chemises of the Civil War era to the neon nylon stockings of the go-go years—is definitely worth talking about. In every stitch, there is a story.

The trove of women’s bloomers, drawers, knickers, brassieres, corsets, and girdles is just a small part of the school’s historic clothing collection, with images shared by the University of Wyoming Libraries via JSTOR. Taken together, the intimates trace a timeline of scientific innovation, societal progress, and sometimes surprising aesthetic choices.

White Chemise, ca. 1860. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Yellow Nylon Stockings from the 1960s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Off-white Stockings, ca. 1900. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Black Stockings from the 1910s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
White Mesh Stockings from the 1920s. Click on the image to take a closer look.

Here you can step through history in stockings. While the Victorian woman who wore that white cotton chemise would have hidden her often-colorful stockings beneath enormous crinolines, offering the barest hint of ankle, the turn-of-the-century woman, in her narrower skirts, knew her shins would be on display when she lifted her hem slightly to climb stairs. Hers might be embroidered with delicate flowers. In the 1910s, hems rose a few inches higher—in a practical and patriotic response to the Great War—and opaque fine mesh styles in geometric patterns became popular. Less than a decade later, wide mesh stockings were a signature look for the flapper, with her skirts hemmed just below the knee.

The flapper style was as functional as it was scandalous; the holes that allowed skin to show through also gave the fabric the stretch necessary for dancing. In 1940 came the invention of nylon undergarments, which meant women of the midcentury could be more comfortable and less revealing in stockings that mimicked some skin tones. That they were followed by their younger sisters in bright, glittering stockings under miniskirts in the 1960s makes a lot more sense when you know what came before.

Peach Cami-Knickers from the 1920s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Black Bloomers from the 1900s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Undergarment Envelope Combination from the 1910s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
White Under-split Drawers from the 1890s. Click on the image to take a closer look.

In the collection, you can also see the literal foundations of women’s everyday lives through the decades. A pair of billowy, pleated black bloomers that would have looked a lot like drawers to earlier generations meant freedom to New Women of the 1900s, who bicycled and played sports in the once-scandalous attire. The 1910s envelope combination, a one-piece garment that combined the chemise and drawers, reshaped women’s lives, slimming down the stereotypical silhouette. In the 1920s, the envelope combination evolved into cami-knickers, the undergarment that would define the postwar Jazz Age. Loose, tube-shaped cami-knickers created the boyish shape favored by flappers, and silky, slinky fabrics like crepe de chine added modern allure to once-utilitarian pieces.

Expectations of women—and their underwear—changed yet again after the Second World War. In 1947, French fashion designer Christian Dior debuted a curvy, hourglass style that emphasized a full bust, cinched waist, and sloping hips. The designs were a backlash against the boxy, tailored uniforms of the war era and soon became known as the “New Look”—though any student of fashion history would have recognized the silhouette as a throwback to the previous century. With this new trend came a demand for all-in-one girdles, which shaped the body from bust to hips with elasticized panels and boning, and half slips, which continued the smooth illusion through the upper legs.

Browsing the virtual closets of the University of Wyoming, you can assemble an outfit piece by piece. Start with a green ruffled cocktail dress and a veiled black hat, then add a small black clutch and black stilettos designed by Palter DeLiso, until the full picture of a real woman and her story emerges from countless yards and yards of fabric.

item.title: What Civics Class Is For
item.content:encoded:
公民教育 民主 争议政治议题 伦理 教师榜样

总结:
1. 文章回顾了一个多世纪前美国关于公立学校如何更好培养好公民的讨论，并提到早在1903年就有学者指出，“公民学”一词仅约15年历史，相关实践更年轻。
2. 与今天把学校重点放在职业培训不同，福曼认为培养好公民是学校的首要职能。
3. 他批评公民课教师常回避当时具体政治争议，认为这是错误的，学生应理解未来作为选民会遇到的问题。
4. 他主张公民教育应鼓励学生思考民主，包括民主思想史、实际治理、保护少数群体、理解联邦制、制衡与公民自由，同时了解地方、州和联邦机构运作，但不能只讲机械治理，否则学生会觉得公民课最枯燥无用。
5. 他还强调公民教育应触及伦理，但不依赖不适合课堂的宗教论证，而应以教师的道德价值观、行为和品格作为榜样，因为正确投票需要头脑与心灵的结合，否则可能只是培养更聪明成功的公共恶棍。

For more than a century, Americans have commonly asked how public schools could do a better job of teaching people to be good citizens. One early stab at the question came from S. E. Forman, an early advocate for civics education. Writing in 1903, he noted that it was no surprise things hadn’t been ironed out yet, since the word civics “is only about fifteen years old and the thing is even younger.”

In marked contrast to today’s focus on school as training for future employment, Forman wrote that “we are told in season and out of season” that training for good citizenship “is the chief function of the school.”

Forman was distressed to find that civics teachers often avoided looking at specific political issues of the day, judging them to be too controversial.

Forman argued that civics should begin by encouraging students to “think as much as possible about democracy.” This included understanding the history of democratic ideas and practical governance, as well as the need to protect minority groups and the dangers posed by demagogues.

Along with understanding the “spirit” of democracy, he wrote, students should understand its principles, including federalism, checks and balances, and civil liberty. He also noted the need to teach how the US government is organized, including the workings of various bodies at the local, state, and national levels. However, he argued that the civics classes of his time were altogether too focused on the mechanical aspects of governance, much to the dismay of students.

“In the acquisition of this knowledge they come to look upon civics as the driest, the most unprofitable, and the most stupid of all their studies,” Forman wrote. “And their impressions are often just.”

More to Explore

The Case for Lowering the Voting Age

Livia Gershon
October 17, 2018
If the standard we hold for who can vote is the consent of the governed, why shouldn’t children be included?

Forman was also distressed to find that civics teachers often avoided looking at specific political issues of the day, judging them to be too controversial. He suggested that this was a mistake and that it’s crucial for students to understand the topics that will come before them as voters.

He praised one high school teacher he had watched present a lesson on tariffs. At the time, this was a key issue in a presidential election. While the class was divided between protectionists and free-traders, the teacher gave no indication of his own views, and the textbook presented objective facts along with arguments from both sides. The point, Forman suggested, was not to change anyone’s mind but to encourage better understanding and clearer thinking.

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Finally, Forman argued that civics must touch on ethics, but without leaning on religious arguments inappropriate for the classroom. Instead, he viewed teachers’ own moral values, conduct, and character as key to presenting students with a model of decency.

“To vote right requires a happy union of head and heart,” he wrote. “And if instruction in civics does not effect this union, as likely as not its chief result will be to prepare many of the learners for more successful and intelligent careers as public rogues.”

item.title: The Jewish Labor Bund’s Anti-Zionist Legacy
item.content:encoded:
Molly Crabapple’s new best-seller, Here Where We Live is Our Country: The Story of the Jewish Labor Bund tells the nearly lost history of the “most influential Jewish political force in eastern Europe.” In the first two decades of the twentieth century, the General Jewish Labor Bund in Lithuania, Poland, and Russia—the places where the majority of Jews in the world then lived—was secular, socialist, and “uncompromisingly anti-Zionist.”

Zionism, the movement for a “Jewish homeland,” was antithetical to the Bundists’ sense of community, doikayt (Yiddish for “hereness”), succinctly summarized in Crabapple’s title: here where we live is our country. Migration to a thereness, or dorkayt, in the Middle East was the wrong path in the eyes of Bundists. The Bund was formed in 1897, the same year the First Zionist Congress was held to begin the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine.

During the “red decade” of the 1930s, more Jews passed through membership in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) than through the liberal American Jewish Committee.

This history complicates the contemporary argument that anti-Zionism is necessarily antisemitic: some Jewish political movements, including the Bund, were themselves explicitly anti-Zionist.

The Bund didn’t survive Hitler and Stalin, but its legacy lived on, particularly among Eastern European Jews who migrated to the United States before the racially discriminatory national origins immigration quotas of 1924. Cultural studies scholar Benjamin Balthaser takes up the Jewish anti-Zionist legacy in Citizens of the Whole World: Anti-Zionism and the Cultures of the American Jewish Left. For the Bund, writes Balthaser in American Quarterly:

Zionism’s “separatist, chauvinist, clerical, and conservative” culture was understood as the “polar opposite” of the radical Yiddish-speaking organizations of Europe that were progressive, secular, and internationalist.

American Jews between the world wars were predominantly working class and left-wing. Balthaser describes how they were despised by the dominant Protestant culture as a “biopolitical” threat, the “most racially alien” and “unassimilable” of immigrants. Balthaser also notes that during the “red decade” of the 1930s, more Jews passed through membership in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) than through the liberal American Jewish Committee. For these Jews, calls for the creation of a new Zion was petit-bourgeois, right-wing nationalist, and imperialist, “directly or indirectly requiring the support of the British Empire.”

For Jewish communists, the promised land was communism, not what the CPUSA called the “Jim Crowism” of Jewish-only settlements.

More to Explore

Israel and Gaza: A Syllabus of Background Readings

The Editors
October 19, 2023
How can we help students begin to make sense of the current and recurring violence in Israel and Gaza?

Even the resolutely non-communist Hannah Arendt, as late as 1945, saw Zionism as an elite collaboration with European imperialism that would “pass over” the “genuine national revolutionary movement which sprang from the Jewish masses.”

In 1947, the Soviet Union, writes Balthaser, “which had either sided with Palestinian anti-colonial revolts or at least was ambiguous enough so that local and national Communist Parties often went their own way,” came out in support of Partition. This was the UN plan to split British Mandate Palestine into Arab and Jewish states. Followers of the Moscow “line” suddenly switched from “advocating a binational, democratic state to supporting a single Jewish state.”

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

The 1948 Arab–Israeli War culminated in the establishment of Israel and the expulsion of nearly 700,000 Palestinians from their homes. Balthaser connects that history to what he describes as decades of Palestinian “displacement and state violence” and, since 1967, Israel’s “settler colonial project.”

For Balthaser, these developments bore out some of the Jewish left’s warnings about Zionism as a project of nationalism, imperialism, and ethnic exclusion. He argues that the “wide-spread opposition of working-class and left-wing US Jews to Zionism during the 1930s and most of the 1940s” was largely forgotten in the following decades as Zionism was claimed to “represent the unified interests or will of ‘the Jewish people.’”

But the legacy of Jewish anti-Zionism has been reawakened in the work cited here, and in the writings of Peter Beinart, Judith Butler, Naomi Klein, Shaul Magid, and others, as well as, more collectively, in organizations like Jewish Voice for Peace, IfNotNow, and a reborn Jewish Labor Bund.

item.title: Why Is Leadership Riskier for Women?
item.content:encoded:
Two competing theories are frequently offered to explain why women are dramatically underrepresented in the highest leadership positions, from Congress to Fortune 500 companies. Some argue that cultural norms of male leadership and even outright discrimination keep women from top roles, while others argue that women are less ambitious than men. These explanations may not be mutually exclusive, though. Research by Susan R. Fisk and Jon Overton shows that women’s leadership ambitions are depressed by the expectation that women will be disproportionately penalized for failures.

Fisk and Overton use three surveys to trace how expectations of harsher penalties for failure can dampen women’s leadership ambitions. First, they find that both women and men—but women to a greater degree—”believe that women leaders face greater sanctions for failure than otherwise similar men.” There’s good reason for that belief. Research has found, for example, that “women managers are formally penalized more harshly for committing an ethical violation than otherwise similar men managers” and “women surgeons receive a sharper drop in referrals when a patient dies than male surgeons.” Fisk and Overton’s findings suggest that this phenomenon is common knowledge.

Harsher sanctions for women leaders when things go wrong can discourage women from seeking those roles in the first place.

Second, they asked respondents to consider whether they would take on a professional leadership role with a high risk of failure. Half of the respondents were told that failure would not affect their careers: they could return to their current team and could count on support from their manager. The other half were told that failure could mean losing their job and that their manager had not pledged support. Both men and women were less likely to say they wanted the leadership role when failure carried these risks—but the effect was stronger for women.

More to Explore

How Gender Discrimination Works at Work

Laura Clawson
February 20, 2026
A study of employment discrimination cases reveals how bias operates through workplace rules.

The final study used the same scenario as the second, but added additional controls and questions to test whether women’s lower interest in a risky leadership role could be linked to their expectation of greater sanctions for failure—and to rule out alternative explanations. The research found that “anticipated sanctions account for about 31 percent of the decrease in women’s leadership ambitions.”

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

It is true, then, that women can be less likely than men to have leadership ambitions. But that is not simply an innate difference. Rather, to a significant extent, it can be a response to the greater risk women face in leadership positions. As a result, harsher sanctions for women leaders when things go wrong can discourage women from seeking those roles in the first place. As Fisk and Overton write, “gender discrimination against women leaders not only harms women leaders: this discrimination also decreases the likelihood that women pursue leadership positions in the first place.”

The post Why Is Leadership Riskier for Women? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
